Caesium (or cesium) is the chemical element with the atomic number 55 on the periodic table. Its symbol is Cs. Caesium is an alkali metal. Its melting point is low (28 °C). It is extremely reactive. Because of its high reactivity, it is a dangerous chemical. It may set itself on fire (ignite) in air. It explodes on contact with water. It reacts more violently than the other alkali metals with water. Because of this, caesium is stored in mineral oil. Caesium is a rare element. Since there is little caesium on the Earth, it is rather expensive. The human body does not need caesium. In large amounts, its chemical compounds are mildly poisonous because it is close to potassium, which the body does need. Caesium was first described in 1860, by Gustav Robert Kirchhoff and Robert Wilhelm Bunsen. They were testing mineral water, from Bad Dürkheim in Rhineland-Palatinate. After they separated calcium, strontium, magnesium and lithium, they saw two lines in the "blue" range of the spectrum. Because of these lines, they concluded that in addition to the elements already found, there must be another unknown substance in the mineral water. They named this substance caesium, after the color blue. Caesium has at least 39 known isotopes ranging in atomic mass from 112 to 151. Only one of these, Cs, is stable. Therefore, the naturally-occurring isotope of caesium is Cs, which is not radioactive. Cs is used in atomic clocks, its vibration frequency used to define the length of the second. Another isotope, Cs is not made naturally but is made after nuclear fission has been done. It is very radioactive and used as an industrial gamma ray source. Caesium forms compounds with many other chemical elements. Caesium formate is used in oil drilling because of its high density. Caesium is extremely reactive in air and water. Caesium rapidly oxidizes in air and can spontaneously combust (randomly catch on fire) at any moment. For this reason, it must be stored in kerosene or a mineral oil, like other group one elements (lithium, sodium, rubidium, and francium.) In water, caesium violently reacts to make caesium hydroxide (2CsOH). The Caesium sinks for about one second, then explodes. The explosion is over 50 times the size of the element dropped in the water, and the explosion is enough to break a common Pyrex beaker, flask, or test tube.

Caesium 137 is an isotope of caesium. It is radioactive. It is often a by-product of nuclear fission. It has a half life of about 30 years. Many areas where nuclear accidents have occurred, such as Chernobyl and Fukushima, are contaminated with caesium-137.

Caesium iodide is an ionic compound made of caesium and iodide ions. The chemical formula is CsI. It has a molar mass of around 259.81 g/mol. The melting point of caesium iodide is around 632 °C. It is made when caesium (metal or basic compound) reacts with iodine or hydroiodic acid. It can be made when caesium metal reacts with elemental iodine to make caesium iodide. It can also be made when caesium hydroxide reacts with hydroiodic acid to make caesium iodide and water.
Caesium telluride is a chemical compound made of caesium and telluride ions. Its chemical formula is. The molar mass is around 393.41 g/mol. It is used to make photocathodes.

Calcium is a chemical element. Its symbol on the periodic table (a list of all the elements) is Ca. and its atomic number is 20. The atomic number says where Calcium sits in the periodic table. It has 20 protons and 20 electrons (if is an atom, see ion). The most common isotopes are Ca-40 and Ca-44. Its mass number is about 40.07. Calcium is not found as a metal in the ground (a native element mineral) because it is too reactive. Calcium carbonate, also known as calcite, is the most common calcium mineral. Calcium is very important in the human body, for making bones and is an inorganic component found in bones, alongside phosphate. 99% of calcium in the bone is stored in bones. It is used in nerve and muscle (including the heart muscle) contraction. The name comes "calx", the Latin name for lime, or limestone. Calcium is a soft white-gray opaque metal. It is solid at room temperature. The crystal structure of calcium metal changes between two allotropes, being face-centred cubic at room temperature and body-centred cubic above 464 C. It melts at 842 C. It does not conduct electricity as well as copper, but is much lighter in weight. Calcium is the third alkaline earth metal, and has similar chemistry to the rest of the group. It is a strong reducing agent and base with two valence electrons. Calcium metal reacts with oxygen in the air to make a layer of calcium oxide on the outside of the metal. This stops further chemical reactions (passivation) until the layer is removed. This compound is a strong Brønsted base and reacts with Brønsted acids to make calcium salts of the conjugate base. Non-passivated calcium metal can also make salts by reducing Brønsted acids directly to hydrogen gas. If the calcium salt of an acid is soluble in that acid or the solvent being used, the calcium-acid reaction is very fast and gives off a lot of heat. Calcium forms chemical compounds in the +2 oxidation state. Calcium compounds are colorless. Most calcium compounds are not toxic. They are needed in the human body, actually. They are unreactive as far as calcium ions go. Calcium oxide was used to make limelights, which have a flame heating calcium oxide and makes it glow very bright. Forms (compounds) of calcium include: Calcium carbonate (used in medications and construction) Calcium bicarbonate (causes limescale, such as on kitchen and bathroom appliances) Calcium sulphate (also called gypsum, used in brewery and construction) Calcium chloride (used in medical treatments and food processing) Calcium hydroxide (used in construction, food processing, and water treatment) Calcium nitride (used in chemistry and making LED lights) Calcium oxide (used in water treatment and metal (steel) work) Calcium oxalate (found in plants for example in stinging nettle during the winter, when it is flowering) Calcium permanganate (used in water treatment, as a disinfectant and for sterilizing) Calcium phosphate (used in medicine, calcium phosphate compounds are used in making wine) Monocalcium phosphate (used in baking, animal feed and fertilizers) Calcium has 6 naturally occurring isotopes (40Ca, 42Ca, 43Ca, 44Ca, 46Ca and 48Ca), of which 48Ca is very slightly radioactive with a half-life about 6.4×1019 years. Traces of 41Ca, 45Ca and 47Ca are made by cosmic rays striking atoms, and are called cosmogenic nuclides. 41Ca is made by the neutron activation of 40Ca in the upper layers of the Earth's crust and has a half-life of 102,000 years. Since it decays to potassium-41, it is a critical indicator of solar system anomalies. Calcium-40 is the most abundant isotope (96% of all natural calcium), since it comes from radiogenic 40K, which has a half-life of 1.25 billion years. However, along with calcium-46, it is theoretically unstable but with a half-life so long it has never been observed to decay. Calcium is found in high amounts in soil, especially when the soil has been made from rocks high in the different calcium forms. It can be deposited into the soil over time by leaching and deposition. It comes from rainfall and leaching out of the atmosphere, and it probably plays a role in the water cycle (or rain cycle). Because calcium is so porous (which means water can go through it), the soil could use it on some layer as a natural filter. Leaching also causes calcium to go from the rain into human drinking water in some parts of the world, and causes "hard" drinking water, in places where there is a lot of calcium in the environment and water. When calcium is mixed into building materials in the right form and concentration, it makes buildings stronger and more resistant to weather. Calcium is used by humans in construction (as limestone, or calcium carbonate) to make concrete and bricks better for building with, and gypsum (calcium sulfate) as a plaster. In brewery (making alcohol) gypsum is used and is the good one. Gypsum (calcium sulphate) is the good mineral because it does not break down with boiling, which alcohol needs. Chalk (calcium bicarbonate) is the bad form to use in brewery because it does break down, deposits limescale on the equipment and brings out the "harsher characteristics" of the hops as well as its ions interacting negatively with the fermentation process. Humans (and other animals) use calcium to maintain or grow healthy bones and teeth. Calcium is used in the body where electricity is used, like in the muscles and nerves. Calcium is useful for animals and humans, and is found in nature. Cow milk is rich in calcium and other nutrients so that baby cows drinking it from their mother can grow up healthy and strong. As an element, calcium is used in the reduction of other metals. It can also be used to make alloys (metal mix) with other metals. Calcium compounds are also important in chemistry. It is important for making things. It is a part of cement which is needed to make concrete (a hard substance that many buildings are made from.) Calcium is part of calcium oxide. Calcium oxide is used to make paper, pottery, food, and to purify water (make it good to drink.) Calcium carbonate is used as a calcium supplement. Calcium permanganate can be used as a rocket propellant. Calcium is used in supplements a lot to increase the size of the tablet (as a bulking agent), for example 500mg of calcium added to in vitamin D tablets or other vitamin supplements. Usually it is in the form of calcium carbonate or calcium citrate. Calcium is added to some medications such as over-the-counter (OTC) antacid products (used to neutralize stomach acid). Calcium has the ability to neutralize stomach acid and some products (like Tums and Rolands, in America) have added calcium in the form of calcium carbonate. The calcium content depends on the antacid product strength and can range from 270-400mg of calcium. Calcium supplements exist and taking less than 1,500mg a day is probably not going to cause harm. Taking too much calcium in supplement form might damage the body, and a balanced, varied diet is usually enough to get all of the calcium the body needs. Supplements are taken with food. Some people have adverse reactions to calcium supplements, or more rarely, allergic reactions. Signs of adverse effects from calcium supplements (or hypercalcaemia) include feeling tired, confused, headache, an upset stomach (or tummy ache), constipation and throwing up. Calcium can cause bone pain in high amounts or as an allergic or adverse reaction. Calcium as an element is not found in the human body, just calcium ions in the form of chemical compounds. In this form it is used in the body. People usually get enough calcium from the diet. Adult humans (aged 19 to 64) need around 700mg of calcium daily. Calcium is used throughout the human body, used in most muscles. Taking 1,500mg of calcium (usually as a supplement in these amounts) is unlikely to cause harm. Dietary calcium comes from milk and dairy products or soya drinks with added calcium, fish where eating them includes the bones (for example, sardines), and green, leafy vegetables. Vegetables that are high in calcium include curly kale and okra, but not spinach (which does contain a lot of calcium but it is not useful for the body). Fortified flour which makes bread (called fortified food) might be a source of calcium or other the fortifying additives (such as niacin or vitamin B3) it contains. Calcium metal is made by electrolysis, usually with melted calcium chloride in a molten salt bath. It has to be very hot to melt it. The reaction occurs in the range of 650 to 750 degrees celsius (C) (around 1200 to 1560 degrees fahrenheit). Sometimes, additives are used to lower the boiling point of the metal. This is because pure calcium chloride melts at around 772 C, or calcium chloride melts in the range of 772 to 782 degrees celsius. Potassium chloride can be used as an additive for the preparation of calcium chloride via electrolysis. It make the extraction more efficient by lowering its boiling point. The amount of potassium added to the molten salt bath can range from 15 to 35 percent (with 75 percent calcium chloride), with 10 percent being the minimum or 25 percent being preferred. Calcium is toxic as an element. It reacts with water and makes a strong base, calcium hydroxide. Calcium compounds are not toxic unless the anion is toxic. Calcium permanganate is only toxic because of the permanganate, not the calcium. Like other alkaline earth metals calcium burns easily and brightly.

Calcite is one of the most common minerals on the Earth's surface. It is a often part of sedimentary rocks, especially limestone. It is also the primary mineral in metamorphic marble. It is a chemical or biochemical calcium carbonate with the formula CaCO3. It is a carbonate mineral. It can be a vein mineral in deposits from hot springs, and in caverns as stalactites and stalagmites.

Calcium carbonate is a chemical compound made of calcium and carbonate ions, with the chemical formula CaCO3. The elements involved are calcium (Ca), carbon (C), and oxygen (O). It is a common substance found as rock in all parts of the world, and is the main component of seashells, snails, and eggshell. Calcium carbonate is usually the main cause of hard water. It is used as a calcium supplement or as a treatment for antacid (brand name Tums), but too much can be bad for your health. Calcium carbonate is found naturally as the following minerals and rocks: Calcium carbonate reacts with strong acids (like hydrochloric acid) to make calcium salt, water, and carbon dioxide. It can also react with weak acids (like acetic acid) but less quickly. All of the rocks and minerals mentioned above will react with acids. The balanced chemical equation of calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid reaction is: The word chemical equation for the hydrochloric acid reaction is: While the balanced chemical equation of calcium carbonate and acetic acid reaction is: And the word chemical equation for the acetic acid reaction is: This is why a rock or mineral might need to be added with an acid to check there is calcium carbonate or not. If there is, then it will fizz and make carbon dioxide. But if it does not, then it will not fizz because there is no carbon dioxide forming.

Calcium bromate is a chemical compound. Its chemical formula is Ca(BrO3)2. It contains calcium and bromate ions. Calcium bromate is a colorless solid. It dissolves in water easily. It is an oxidizing agent. It is similar to calcium chloride. It is made by oxidation (by electrolysis) of calcium bromide solution. It can also be made by dissolving bromine in hot calcium hydroxide solution. This also makes calcium bromide. It is added to flour to make it better in some areas.

Calcination is a process where a chemical compound is heated to high temperatures while exposed to air. Calcination is a type of thermal decomposition. The name "calcination" comes from the Latin word "calcinare", meaning "to burn limestone". Production of quicklime by calcination is one of the oldest known chemical reactions.

Calcium helps makes the bones and teeth stronger as well as playing a part in blood clotting. Calcium is a dietary mineral. Inside the body (as dietary calcium) it is used as calcium ions in the form of chemical compounds. More than 99% of the calcium in the body is stored in bones, which is stored and released using chemical signalling. Adults (aged 19-64) need 700mg of calcium a day, according to the NHS (National Health Service in the UK). In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) sets the recommended daily allowance (RDA) for adults and children over the age of 4 at 1,300mg. Human beings can usually get the dietary calcium they need from eating a healthy, balanced diet. Calcium is best known for keeping the teeth and bones strong. Other things that it does in the body is causing muscle contraction, including the heart muscle. In the heart, contraction is called systole, and other muscles contract by getting shorter. In muscles it causes the contraction to stay on, because it affects the polarity (and flow of other minerals, like salt and potassium) of the cell. Calcium has a role in cells throughout the body including in nerves, and in pregnancy and apoptosis. It is tightly regulated and interacts with fluoride and phosphor in the blood and bones, plays a role in gut (intestine) health (interacting with other minerals such as magnesium there), and is relevant in some types of drug metabolism. Calcium also helps with blood clotting. Calcium is an inorganic part of the bone matrix, which includes other inorganic components like phosphate and hydroxide ions. Dietary calcium is found in ample (enough) amounts in a balanced diet. Usually, humans can get enough calcium daily from diet alone, but people who are at risk or cannot eat a balanced diet can use supplements to get their recommended daily allowance (RDA). Taking more than 1,500mg of calcium a day can sometimes cause diarrhoea. Usually, supplements are the cause of the body having too much calcium. 1,500mg or less of daily calcium is not likely to cause harm. Soya drinks (soy milk) with added calcium Fish where the bones are eaten (like sardines for example) Green, leafy vegetables (like okra and curly kale, broccoli, but not spinach, which is only 5% bioactive in most people) Foods that have been fortified with calcium (called fortified foods) include flour. When fortified flour is used to make bread, it becomes a source of calcium. Other fortified foods include cereals and anything made with fortified flour. In the United States, fruit juice drinks are fortified. Fortified foods such as cereals, as well as dairy products, like milk and cheese, or yogurt, are high in calcium which can be used by the body. The calcium absorption of these foods is around 30%. The source of calcium (from foods) changes how much of the calcium is used by the body. Calcium from milk, foods made from milk (such as cheese) and fortified foods are higher than in plant foods, and this is the same with some vitamins (such as vitamin A). Foods like plants or vegetables, such as leafy green vegetables, like Chinese cabbage or broccoli or spinach, are high in calcium but form (create) salt compounds which cannot be digested by the body. Oxalic acid and phytic acid are two examples of compounds found in plants which interact with calcium to form salts that are not bioactive. The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey in America found that some people get less calcium from their diet than they need then other groups of people. It found that black and Asian people living in America who are not hispanic and poor people are less likely than other people to be getting enough dietary calcium. The same study found that in 2007-2010, 49% of children were not getting enough calcium, 39% of all people above the age of 4, from food or supplements in America. Other people that might not get enough calcium from diet include vegans or people who do not or cannot drink milk. People that are allergic to milk or have lactose intolerance might not get enough dietary calcium. This includes other people who might be at risk because of their race. In these people, lactose-free dairy products can supplement their diet so that it contains enough calcium that the body can use. Fish that are eaten with the bones are a source of calcium. These people might have to eat fortified foods fortified with calcium in order to reach their recommended daily limit and prevent negative side effects. After menopause, the lack of estrogen in the body causes it to not absorb calcium as well, or cause the body to lose more calcium. In the United States and Europe, about 30% of these women have osteoporosis, and 40% or more of those with the condition get at least 1 bone fracture. This is caused by the increased risk in falls and decreased calcium reabsorption. Compared to women, male increase in fracture risk from age-related bone loss happens 5-10 years later than in women. Too little calcium can cause osteoporosis, fragile bones, increased risk of falls, and increased bone fractures, but these are more commonly caused by a deficiency of vitamin D. Hypoalbuminemia (low blood levels of a protein called albumin) might also look the same as low calcium levels in the blood. Low calcium levels can also cause high blood pressure (hypertension), like hypercalcaemia can. Falls and fractures are common in menopausal women because estrogen helps regulate bone formation and remodelling. Loss of bone density happens to older women during menopause if estrogen levels are left unchecked (with an estrogen deficiency) which can cause pain and problems with mobility. On average, 1% of the bone mineral density is lost per year in these people. People with osteoporosis get fractured bones more often. Low calcium can cause mild cramps. People at risk of this are usually given hormones (hormone replacement therapy, often called HRT) or supplements to prevent bone loss and the problems caused by that. Low calcium also causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in children and adults, or other bone disorders in adults. Low blood serum levels of calcium (hypocalcaemia), measured as blood having less than 8.5mg/dL (mg per decilitre) (2.12mmol/L), or as an ionized calcium level of less than 4.61mg/dL (1.15mmol/L), is usually caused by a deficiency in vitamin D or magnesium. These levels can also be caused by hormonal imbalances, for example if the thyroid hormone (producing parathyroid hormone) is not working properly), causing hypoparathyroidism. It can also be caused by low bone reabsorption or calcium reabsorption, medications or illness. Hypocalcaemia is another symptom of proton pump inhibitor drugs (PPIs), which lower the stomach acid, as well as cisplatin (chemotherapy medication) or bisphosphonate drugs which come as adverse effects. Hypocalcaemia can cause no symptoms (be asymptomatic), especially when the body is only slightly deficient or has been deficient for a long time. Because calcium affects most cells in the body, symptoms of not having enough can range widely between people. Hypocalcaemia can cause neuromuscular irritability including muscle spasms, paraesthesia (tingling in the hands and feet), or perioral (around the mouth) numbness. More serious signs and symptoms can include kidney injury, or calcification, brain calcification, congestive heart failure, cataracts, paraesthesia (numbness or tingling of the fingers or toes), seizures and rarely, coma. Low calcium levels can cause symptoms of mental illness such as depression, anxiety, or bipolar disorder too. Trousseau's sign, the symptom of the hands curling in, the wrists and fingers coming together and flexing tight, can also show when inflating a tourniquet or cuff (used to measure blood pressure). This happens when there is too little calcium in the blood. It might show itself when pumping a cuff or applying a tourniquet to draw blood from the arm. Calcium levels are measured without a cuff, but one might be used to find a nerve and make it easier to put a catheter or needle into the arm (but the blood should not be taken without deflating the cuff). A mnemonic for remembering what shows in calcium deficiency, using the first letters of SPASMOD IC: S - Spasms (Trousseau's sign being carpopedal spasms) P - Perioral (around the mouth) parasthesiae (numbness) A - Anxious, irritable, irrational (mental signs) M - In smooth muscle, an increase in muscle tone (which causes colic, wheeze, dysphagia) O - Orientation impairment (orientation not working properly, like time, place, who the person is) and confusion D - Dermatitis (for example atopic or exfoliative dermatitis) I - Impetigo herpetiformis, happening during pregnancy, rarely, but serious. Causes lower calcium (and pustules, during pregnancy) C - Chvostek's sign (twitching in the corner of the mouth during tests of the facial nerve, testing nerve over-excitement by tapping the parotid) High calcium intake increases the risk of one type of acquired kidney stone disease (renal calculi). Eating too much calcium can cause stomach pain (abdominal pain) and diarrhoea. Severe diarrhoea can cause the body to lose too much calcium and water, causing hypocalcaemia and dehydration, and so can frequent (often) urination. High calcium can also cause constipation. Magnesium also causes diarrhoea (and is used to cause bowel movements in medicine), and severe diarrhoea can also cause hypomagnesemia. These can be an issue in some parts of the world, such as in developing countries, where there is a lot of diarrhoea. Having too much calcium can also cause polyuria, also called frequent urination. In addition to mental illnesses, which come from chronic (long-term) high calcium, for example depression, anxiety, and bipolar disorder, it can cause kidney stones and pyrexia (red skin). Kidney stones are extremely painful. Having too much calcium can cause ectopic (made in the place that it shouldnt be) calcification, like fluorosis. This makes bones form incorrectly. High calcium levels can cause weight loss, being tired, weak (weakness) and mental confusion. High calcium levels can cause hypertension (high blood pressure), like low calcium can. It can also cause cardiac arrest (heart stopping, a type of heart attack), and hypercalcaemia shows on electrocardiograms (ECG) as a shortened QT interval, prolonged (longer) PR interval. Some studies have shown that high calcium intake can make cardiovascular disease (CVD) more likely. The amount of calcium needed depends on age, like the levels needed for it to be too high. These show that high calcium intake may also increase the risk of developing prostate cancer. In America, women take supplements more than men (32% of women compared to 22% of men in the United States). In the same country, 4-8% of children take a supplement. Supplements can be used to treat low calcium levels or for other reasons. A combination form of vitamin D with calcium exist, which contain less than the recommended amount of vitamin D at around 200-400 IU (international units) of vitamin D in these tablets. The dose for calcium supplements is 700mg, but can sometimes be as high as 1000-1300mg of calcium. Taking less than 1,500mg (upper dose limit) of calcium supplements is unlikely to cause harm. Organisms need to keep calcium ion levels very well controlled. High calcium levels are bad, and low calcium levels are In the UK, the normal (physiological) level of calcium (total) in fats, or lipids, is 2.12-2.65mmol/L (millimoles per litre). Tests for calcium levels in blood serum are taken while the patient is fasting (if the doctor has instructed them to be fasting), uncuffed. The tourniquet or cuff can be used to get access to the vein, but it should be taken off before taking the blood sample. Calcium homeostasis is the level of calcium the body needs to keep working, which the body always tries to maintain. Some ways that calcium homeostasis can be maintained are: Calcium is lost in urine. When there is too much calcium, the kidneys can filter it out and excrete it in the urine The thyroid gland is responsible for setting calcium homeostasis, as well as basal metabolic rate Calcium levels in the body are controlled by a thyroid hormone called calcitonin. Calcium levels are lowered by calcitonin The control of calcium in the body is called calcium metabolism. The human body controls calcium levels with many hormones. Calcitonin, Parathyroid hormone (acronym PTH), and Vitamin D are the most important hormones in calcium metabolism. Vitamin D is a vitamin that works as a hormone and it is important in the body as it affects the formation of bones alongside calcium. Most people get enough vitamin D from diet, or have enough of the other vitamins if the glands are working properly. Vitamin D supplements exist, like calcium supplements, but have a higher risk of causing kidney stones than dietary vitamin D. Calcitonin lowers the calcium levels in blood plasma by working with different organs and the bone. It increases calcium excretion from the kidneys, decreases absorption from the gut, and causes more calcium to be stored in bone. When the blood calcium level is high, it stimulates the body, and causes more calcitonin to be excreted, which comes from the C-cells (parafollicular cells). The role that calcitonin has in the body is not obvious. C-cells are thyroid cells that are responsible for making calcitonin. The creation of calcitonin causes a decrease in calcium in phosphate. Opposite to calcitonin, parathyroid hormone raises calcium levels. It is antagonistic to calcitonin, which means it does the opposite things. It lowers the excretion of calcium by the kidneys while increasing bone resorption (which frees up calcium). This causes an increase in calcium. It does this also while making the gut absorb more calcium (by using vitamin D). The parathyroid hormone also causes a decrease in phosphate (as PO43-). Like calcitonin being released when calcium is high, and levels decreasing when calcium goes down, when blood serum levels of calcium rise, the secretion of PTH is decreased. PTH is secretion is triggered by a lowered amount of calcium ions in the blood serum and is controlled by a negative feedback loop, because it makes the amount of calcium in the blood serum rise. During the latent period (the time between reaching the amount needed for muscle contraction and the muscle contracting), the action potential spreads across the muscle and allows calcium to be released (from the SR). If, or when, calcium is released from the sarcoplasm, it is allowed to relax, because calcium is responsible for "holding" the contraction. A simple muscle twitch is the response to a smaller, brief stimulus (getting excited) either at or above the threshold. It is made up of three stages, including the latent period. The other two stages after the latent period are the contraction and relaxation periods. Like how potassium is in a lot of ways the opposite of calcium when talking about cells or metal, phosphor is related when it is calcium and bones. The amount of calcium that is used or stored in bones is linked to the amount of phosphate in blood. Low levels of phosphate (hypophosphatemia) in the blood causes calcium to exit the bones, which then affects the bones negatively. Fluoride can cause bone problems because it acts in the same way as calcium, and leads to fluorosis. When there is too much fluoride in the body, bone formation can go unchecked as well as problems with the kidneys and blood pressure. Alongside calcium, sodium and magnesium, as well as potassium are stored in the bone. Calcium is an inorganic component of the bone matrix, as well as hydroxide ions and phosphate. When bones are being formed in the body, calcium as well as phosphate are sourced from the blood, lowering blood calcium levels. Organic components of the bone structure include collagen, as well as glycoproteins and other peptides. Calcium ions are important to cells, but too many calcium ions can be bad. If a cell gets more calcium ion than it needs, it can die. This is why the amount of calcium ion in cells is highly regulated. At the same time, not enough calcium ion is bad. Cells must have the right amount to function properly. The normal (physiological) level of calcium (total) in fats, or lipids, is 2.12-2.65mmol/L (millimoles per litre). It is measured in the total plasmic Ca2 amount in blood serum (around 40% being together with albumin, and around 60%, or the rest, is free calcium in its ionized form). Things that can affect calcium binding include cirrhosis (of the liver) and different proteins being in the myeloma. The binding of calcium varies from person to person. Cells which use calcium for motility (plant cells also do this) do not usually have calcium move around after the cell has taken it in, and afterwards it is usually discarded. Calcium can bind to fat (called lipids) in the body. Many cells have calcium channels on their membrane surface. These are openings (called invaginations) where calcium ions can enter the cell and do different things. Whether calcium or other minerals can enter the cell or not is dependent on the gate which is open or closed with electricity (polarization). The voltage difference between the inside and outside of the cell makes the voltage-gated channel open or closed, to allow calcium to enter or exit. Once in the cell calcium ions activates many proteins to do specific things. For example, calcium goes into white blood cells and causes them to become motile, to help them move around and fight germs. One type of cell that uses calcium are muscle cells, which includes cells in the heart muscle. When it goes into muscle cells, it makes them contract (shorten so the muscle pulls) and cause it to stay contracted. It could also be said that the opposite of calcium is potassium in cells, and potassium is used in making calcium metal for the same reason. In the body, calcium helps cells stay contracted, while potassium helps them release. The contents of the cell changing to push out or take in calcium and potassium changes its polarity, which allows the cells to keep working. Nitrogen moieties can interact with the voltage-gated calcium channels (because nitrogen and calcium react with one another) and this is one way that compounds such as drugs can interact with the cell. Cyclic AMP (cAMP), or adenosine monophosphate uses nitrogen to interact with cells in this way. Calcium levels increase, or cAMP levels change, in G-coupled receptors to change the polarity, which is used in nerves as well as in drugs. Like cAMP and calcium, inositol triphosphate (IP3) is a chemical messenger. All muscles are able to contract. Muscle contraction depends on calcium as well as ATP (adenosine triphosphate). Depolarization of the muscle causes an action potential, which spreads throughout the muscles, and causes calcium (in the form of Ca2) to be released from the cell. As the action potential (signal) decays, the cells stop releasing calcium and start to take calcium back in. When calcium goes into nerve cells, it triggers electrical impulses that send a message called an action potential. Calcium channels open and allow for calcium to go into the nerve cells when the action potential reaches the nerve terminal. Nerves waiting to be excited are stored in the membrane-bound (in membranes) vesicles. This causes cell depolarization and makes an electrical connection with the reaction that is caused and the electrical conductivity of the mineral. When the amount of calcium in these cells goes up very fast, the nerves on the vesicles that were waiting to be excited join together (fusion) with the cell membrane at the nerve synapse. This fused vesicle membrane that is high in calcium can pass electricity between points because they are touching and filled with calcium. The membrane is filled with neurotransmitters (nerves).This causes the nerve to get excited, which is called exocytosis. In human fertilization, the penetration of the sperm through the membrane of the egg (ovum) called the cortical reaction causes a release of calcium ions. The amount of calcium ions increasing inside the cell depolarizes it, and increases the metabolic rate of the zygote (a diploid type of germ cell) so that it can grow. By depolarizing the cell, the calcium prevents fertilization from multiple sperm cells. The fertilized and depolarized egg is now called the fertilization membrane. Twins come from two different ovum released during the ovulatory cycle being fertilized by two different sperm (which causes non-identical twins), or when a single zygote splits into two (causing identical twins). Sometimes cells are unhealthy and need to die in for the body to replace them with new, healthy cells. This keeps the whole organism healthy. Cells know when they should die and can trigger reactions to end their life cycles in many ways. When this happens it is called apoptosis, also known as a 'programmed cell death' (planned cell death.) One way cells accomplish apoptosis by taking in toxic levels of calcium ions. Age-related bone loss occurs in both men and older women, around 5-10 years later in men. Bone loss can cause osteoporosis or other disorders related to bone. Bone loss can cause rickets in children and osteomalacia in children and people over 4, and other bone-related problems in people over 4. Calcium deficiency increases the risk of bone fractures as well as falls. These fractures can occur in the hip, vertebra and forearms. A hip fracture in a young woman might not be normal (if her calcium levels are high), and bone fractures like these can be caused by an overactive parathyroid gland (releasing too much PTH), causing increased bone reabsorption and more fragile bones. Cancer of the gland might also cause this. In this case the bones might reabsorb calcium from the blood even though levels are already high. Studies have shown that people at risk of falls or bone fractures taking calcium supplements does not decrease their risk, but can reduce bone density loss. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) showed with "moderate certainty" that calcium-vitamin-D supplements do not decrease the risk of fractures happening in postmenopausal women. Vitamin D is closely related to calcium. The ones also rely on vitamin D, which can cause problems with the bones. However, low levels of calcium can mask the signs of vitamin D deficiency as well as magnesium deficiency. When the body does not get enough calcium over a long period of time, or gets only slightly less than it needs, it can also cause no symptoms. Medications can affect the calcium levels in the body. Calcium can also interact with medications. Calcium-Vitamin-D supplements interacts with over 300 medications. For example, it interacts with lithium (a treatment for bipolar disorder) and cause hypercalcemia when taken with calcium supplements, and calcium can interact with levothyroxine (a thyroid hormone, also used to treat thyroid cancer) and cause the drug to be absorbed by the body less. It can interact with a HIV medication used by adults and children called dolutegravir, and cause the levels of the medication in the blood to lowered when taking calcium supplements. Quinolone antibiotics become less effective when they are taken alongside (with) calcium supplements. Examples of quinolone antibiotics include ciprofloxacin, gemifloxacin, moxifloxacin. In a lot of studies, the difference between calcium gained from diet, and from supplements, has to be considered. The difference in calcium from supplements or from eating foods can be significant, and shows that calcium may be different when it is taken in supplemental form like with vitamin D. Studies have shown that lower calcium intake is linked with some heart problems. Low calcium can increase the risk of getting high blood pressure (hypertension), stroke, and thickening of the heart vessels called atherosclerosis. The heart vessels might get narrower because their walls are thicker with cholesterol or plaque. However, in some of the studies, the increased risk is because calcium supplements were used, or that calcium supplements do not increase the risk. Because calcium can join (bind) with fatty acids in the body, it can lower fat (lipids) absorption and then lower the risk of cardiovascular diseases (or CVD). However some studies have shown that it actually increases the risk, including risk of CVD. Diets low in fat and or nonfat dairy products (like 0% milk, also called fat-free milk) and higher than the what the average diet in America has, lowered the systolic blood pressure by 5.5mmHg (millimeters mercury) on average. This meant that the pressure in the blood vessels when the heart was contracted was lower. This could mean that diets low in fat and high in calcium makes the blood pressure lower. The study showed the diastolic blood pressure (when the heart was contracted) was lower by 3.0mmHg on average when the diet was higher than the average calcium, and lower in fat (including from dairy). Metabolic syndrome is a group of at least 3 risk factors for diabetes (which causes high triglyceride levels, high lDL (low density lipoprotein) high fasting (not eating) blood sugar levels (hyperglycemia), and a large waistline), and heart disease and stroke. Studies have shown that metabolic syndrome can be prevented by using calcium supplements, especially in women. Studies showed that women (but less in men) had a lower risk of developing metabolic syndrome when they got their recommended dietary amount of calcium every day. While calcium does not reduce the mortality of cancers like lung, breast, prostate or colorectal cancer, the risk of developing some types of cancer might be lowered by calcium. Though studies gave mixed results, some of them showed that the risk of developing colorectal cancer is lowered by calcium. These results do not always agree with the studies done on calcium supplements. Calcium was seen to decrease the risk of colon cancer by 26% (587mg/day), but not rectal cancer. These studies showed the risk going down by 8% with 300mg/d taken, or 16% with 600mg of increase of daily calcium intake. Prostate cancer risk has been seen to increase with calcium taking in more calcium from diet, but only from dairy foods. Dairy is one of the best sources of calcium, and plant-based sources are less bioavailable. Studies putting calcium together with ovarian cancer showed a lower risk in people getting enough calcium, but the study was not statistically perfect. A risk during pregnancy is pre-eclampsia, which is hypertension and proteinuria (proteins in the urine) or thrombocytopenia. Pregnant women who struggle to get enough calcium in their diet might lower their risk of getting pre-eclampsia (which happens from the second half of pregnancy onwards, in 4% of the population of the United States), but studies showing this sometimes have problems with them. None of the studies for pre-eclampsia used vitamin D alongside the calcium supplements. Many professional or health organizations say that calcium supplements during pregnancy are good and can reduce the risk of developing pre-eclampsia or other related problems. Some examples are the American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology and World Health Organization (WHO). Studies were done in other parts of the world, or health organizations like the Canadian Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy Working Group (Canada), Society of Obstetric Medicine of Australia and New Zealand (Australia, New Zealand), including in Argentina, South Africa, and Zimbabwe for measuring the effect or benefit of calcium on preventing pre-eclampsia.

Calcium chloride is a chemical compound made of calcium and chlorine atoms. It has the formula of CaCl2. It absorbs water from the air and releases heat when it is dissolved in water. It is used as a de-icer on roads to melt the ice. It can be formed by mixture of calcium oxide with hydrochloric acid, but this produces a version that is hydrated (has water molecules attached to it). The anhydrous (no water molecules attached) form is needed most of the time. Calcium chloride is melted at a high temperature and electrolyzed to produce calcium metal.

Calcium hydroxide, also known as slaked lime, is a chemical compound with the formula Ca(OH)2. It dissolves slightly in water. It is a base. It can be made by the chloralkali process. It can be dehydrated (remove the water) to calcium oxide by heat. It can be used to neutralize acidic soils.

Calcium oxide is a chemical compound of calcium and oxygen. Its chemical formula is CaO. It is known as quicklime. It is made in a lime kiln. It releases heat when dissolved in water and changes into calcium hydroxide. It is a white powder. It is also a base. It reacts with acids to make calcium salts. Quicklime is an important ingredient of cement.

Calcium nitride is a chemical compound. Its chemical formula is Ca3N2. It contains calcium and nitride ions. It is a red-brown solid. It reacts with water to make calcium hydroxide and ammonia. It reacts with hydrogen to make calcium hydride and calcium amide. It is made by burning calcium in nitrogen. It is also made when calcium burns in air. It can be used as a source of the reactive nitride ion.

Calcium permanganate is a chemical compound. Its chemical formula is Ca(MnO4)2. It contains calcium and permanganate ions. Calcium permanganate is a dark purple solid. It is a powerful oxidizing agent. It is similar to potassium permanganate. It can catch some organic chemicals like alcohol on fire. It can cause an explosion when mixed with sulfuric acid. This is because manganese(VII) oxide. It can be made by calcium oxide with manganese(IV) oxide and calcium nitrate. It might whiten teeth. It can be used as an oxidizing agent, although potassium permanganate is more common.

Calcium nitrate, also known as Norwegian saltpeter, is a chemical compound. Its chemical formula is Ca(NO3)2. It contains calcium and nitrate ions. Calcium nitrate is a colorless solid. It is an oxidizing agent. It absorbs water from the air. It decomposes to make nitrogen dioxide and calcium oxide when heated. Calcium nitrate is made by reacting calcium hydroxide or calcium carbonate with nitric acid. It is made when nitric acid reacts with calcium phosphate. It can be made by reacting ammonium nitrate and calcium hydroxide. Calcium nitrate is used in fertilizers to add nitrogen to the soil. It can be complexed with urea to make a different nitrogen fertilizer.

Calcium sulfide is a chemical compound made of one calcium atom and one sulfide atom. It has the chemical formula CaS. It is white and forms cubes. It has a high melting point of 2,525 Celsius (4,577 °F; 2,798 Kelvin), and decomposes upon contact with water.

Calcium oxalate is a chemical compound. It is the calcium salt of oxalic acid. It has the chemical formula or. It can be found as a dry form, or one of several hydrates. Calcium oxalate can be found as both a mineral and in living things. Plants can make calcium oxalate out of extra calcium from the soil. In humans, it is the most common chemical in kidney stones. Calcium oxalate is most commonly found as the monohydrate,. As a mineral, this is called whewellite. There are also dihydrate and trihydrate forms. Calcium oxalate occurs naturally in many plants as a way of storing extra calcium. In some species, like pineapples, it forms sharp crystals called raphides. Along with the enzyme bromelain, these crystals may help protect the plants from herbivores. Calcium oxalate is the most common oxalate found in lichens. Calcium oxalate is oxidised into calcium carbonate by living things, especially bacteria. Having too much oxalate in the body is called hyperoxaluria, and can lead to a kidney failure called oxalosis. Oxalate is absorbed by water during cooking, with boiling being the most effective. Calcium oxalate in urine can crystallise into kidney stones. Calcium oxalate is a metabolite of ethylene glycol and is involved in ethylene glycol poisoning.

Calcium chlorate is an ionic compound made of calcium and chlorate ions. The chemical formula is. The molar mass is around 206.98 g/mol (anhydrous). Like other chlorates, it is a strong oxidizer. It used as a non-selective herbicide just like sodium chlorate. It can form the dihydrate salt when exposed to moisture or water. It can be made when calcium (metal or basic compound) reacts with chloric acid. It is usually made when hot suspension of calcium hydroxide in water reacts with excess chlorine gas when heated; making calcium chlorate, calcium chloride, and water. It sometimes can be made when calcium hydroxide reacts with chloric acid to make calcium chlorate and water. It decomposes at high temperatures to make calcium chloride and oxygen gas.

Calcium sulfate is a chemical compound with the chemical formula. This compound contains calcium and sulfate ions. Its molar mass is around 136.141 g/mol (anhydrous). It can form the dihydrate (gypsum) or hemihydrate (plaster of Paris) salt when hydrated (depending how much water it has absorbed from the moisture and the temperature). It used as a building material in drywall, an ingredient in Portland cement, a food additive in some foods, and for soil in plant growth due to nutrient sources of calcium and sulfur. It is made when calcium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid to make calcium sulfate dihydrate. Then it hydrates to calcium sulfate dihydrate: It can be dehydrated by heating, which turns calcium sulfate dihydrate or hemihydrate into calcium sulfate anhydrous. Calcium phosphide is a chemical compound made of calcium and phosphide ions. The chemical formula is. The molar mass is around 182.18 g/mol. It appears as a red-brown solid. It is used as rodenticide, fumigant, and preparation of fireworks and flares due to phosphine gas. It can be made when calcium metal reacts with phosphorus to make calcium phosphide. When calcium phosphide reacts with water, it makes calcium hydroxide and phosphine gas.

Californium is a chemical element. It is a radioactive metal. It has the chemical symbol Cf. It has the atomic number 98. Californium is a transuranium element. Californium does not have many uses. It was discovered by bombarding a curium target with alpha particles (helium ions). Californium is named after the US State of California, where it was discovered, in the University of Berkeley. Californium is produced in nuclear reactors and particle accelerators. There are 20 known isotopes. The most stable is californium-251, which has a half-life of 898 years. This short half-life means the element is not found in the Earth's crust. Californium-252, whose half-life is 2.645 years, is the most common isotope used. Compounds of californium are mostly of californium(III), which can take part in three chemical bonds. Californium can be used to help start up nuclear reactors, and is used as a source of neutrons. It can be used in making higher mass elements. Oganesson was synthesized by bombarding californium-249 atoms with calcium-48 ions. When californium is used, workers must be protected from the element's ability to disrupt the formation of red blood cells.

The California newt (Taricha torosa) is a species of newts. They are also called the orange bellied newt. They can grow to 8 inches (20 cm) in length. They have toxic skin. Because of this, the only predator of the California newt are garter snakes. California newts lives in California.
A calorimeter is a tool that measures the amount of thermal energy contained in a substance, or released in a reaction. A commonplace use is to measure heat of combustion.

Calm is an adjective meaning peaceful, quiet; particularly used of the weather, free from wind or storm, or of the sea, opposed to rough. The word appears in French calme, through which it came into English, in Spanish, Portuguese and Italian calma.

The calorie is a pre-SI unit of energy, synonymous with heat. A calorie is defined as the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one gram of water (specific heat capacity = 4,184 J kg-1 K-1) by one K (= °C + 273). On food labels, calorie refers to kilocalories (kilo- = 103), which equals to 1000 calories. As such, the word calorie is usually written with a capital C. In simple words, calories are a way to measure energy. Our bodies get calories from the food we eat. If we eat more calories than we use, the body stores the extra energy as fat. How the body uses a calorie can depend on whether it comes from fat, protein, or carbohydrates.

The Calvin cycle (also known as the Benson-Calvin cycle) is the set of chemical reactions that take place in chloroplasts during photosynthesis. The cycle is light-independent because it takes place after the energy has been captured from sunlight. The Calvin cycle is named after Melvin Calvin, who won a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for finding it in 1961. Calvin and his colleagues, Andrew Benson and James Bassham, did the work at the University of California, Berkeley. Using the radioactive carbon-14 isotope as a tracer, Calvin, Andrew Benson and their team mapped the complete route that carbon travels through a plant during photosynthesis. They traced the carbon-14 from soaking up its atmospheric carbon dioxide to its conversion into carbohydrates and other organic compounds. The single-celled algae Chlorella was used to trace the carbon-14. The Calvin group showed that sunlight acts on the chlorophyll in a plant to fuel the manufacture of organic compounds, not directly on carbon dioxide as previously believed. 1. Grab: A five-carbon carbon catcher called RuBP (Ribulose bisphosphate) catches one molecule of carbon dioxide and forms a six-carbon molecule. 2. Split: the enzyme RuBisCO (with the energy of ATP and NADPH molecules) breaks the six-carbon molecule into two equal parts. 3. Leave: A trio of carbons leave and become sugar. The other trio moves on to the next step. 4. Switch: Using ATP and NADPH, the three-carbon molecule is changed into a five-carbon molecule. 5. The cycle starts over again. The carbohydrate products of the Calvin cycle are three-carbon sugar phosphate molecules, or 'glucose triose phosphates' (G3P). Each step of the cycle has its own enzyme which speeds up the reaction.

Camels are mammals of the Camelidae family. Camels form the genus Camelus. There are three living species of camels. Best-known are the dromedary (one hump) and Bactrian (two humps) camels. The camelids, as a family, include the "New World" camelids: the llama, the alpaca, the guanaco, and the vicuña. The earliest known camel, called Protylopus, lived in North America 40 to 50 million years ago, during the Eocene. It was about the size of a rabbit and lived in the open woodlands of what is now South Dakota. Camels live in deserts, where it is hot and dry. Camels have adapted and found ways to help them survive in deserts. They have a thick coat of hair that protects them from the heat in the day, and keeps them warm at night. Their large feet spread out their weight on the sand when they are walking, so they do not sink into the sand. When there is food and water, a camel can eat and drink large amounts of it and store it as fat in the hump. Then, when there is no food or water, the camel uses the fat for energy, and the hump becomes small and soft. A camel’s waste contains very little water. Even the water from the camel’s breath flows back into its mouth. The camels have bushy eyebrows that don't let the sand go in their eyes in a sandstorm. It has a long slender neck in order to reach high leaves such as palm trees, and rubbery patches on the belly and knees to protect the skin when kneeling and sitting on the hot sand. These form after five years of age. A camel has a naturally adapted temperature regulation - it can change its bodily temperature by six degrees Celsius either way. It has two sets of eyelashes, closing muscles in the nasal passages, hairy ears and tough, leathery skin to protect the camels skin in sandstorms. It has thick rubbery lips to eat dry, prickly plants and a large, haired tail to swat pests such as mosquitos and flies. Camels live in groups, called herds. Herds usually have one male, many females, and their young, called calves. They are animals that use their hooves. An unborn camel gestates about 9 to 11 months. There is usually one calf per birth. A camel calf can run only a few hours after it is born. Calves are weaned to when they are about 1 year old. In the desert, people feed camels with grass, grains, wheat and oats. When camels are travelling in the desert, food is often very hard to find. So the animal might have to live on dried leaves, seeds, and thorny twigs (without hurting their mouths). If there is not any regular food, camels will eat anything. Camels are ruminants, which have a two-part cycle in their eating. The first stomach ferments the food for a time. Then, this food (or cud) returns to the camel's mouth, and the camel chews it again. Then the camel swallows the cud and it goes to the other parts of the stomach to be completely digested. The digestion is done mainly by microorganisms in the stomachs. This adaptation means they can eat food which may not be very nutritious, but they get everything possible out of it. Ruminants are a very successful group of mammals, and this double-stomach arrangement is one of their key adaptations. Most of them eat fairly tough plant material. Camels have been domesticated by humans for about 5000 years. They are used for riding and to carry things, and for meat, milk and wool. As domesticated animals, they are used in Africa, Asia, and since the 19th century also in Australia. About 900-1000 wild Bactrian Camels still live in China, Tibetan Plateau and Mongolia. There are no wild dromedaries anymore, but there are escaped domestic dromedaries in Australia. Today there are dromedaries living wild in the outback in Australia.

CamelCase (camel case, camel caps or medial capitals) is the practice of writing compound words or phrases so that each next word or abbreviation begins with a capital letter. CamelCase can either start with a lowercase or uppercase letter, although the lowercase version is much more common in programming. Common examples are PowerPoint or iPhone. There are many variations of CamelCase. A few important ones are: CapitalizedWords or CapWords for upper CamelCase in Python InterCaps or intercapping (abbreviation of Internal Capitalization) WikiWord or WikiCase (especially in older wikis) The first use of medial capitals was the notation for chemical formulae invented by the Swedish chemist Berzelius in 1813. He did this to replace the many naming and symbol systems used by chemists at that time. He suggested to show each chemical element by a symbol of one or two letters, the first one being capitalized. The capitalization allowed formulae like 'NaCl' to be written without spaces and still be read without confusion. This system is still in use today. Since the early 20th century, medial capitals have occasionally been used for corporate names and product trademarks, such as CinemaScope and VistaVision, rival widescreen movie formats (1953) MisterRogers, the Canadian version of Mister Rogers' Neighborhood (1962) Despite its unclear origins inside the computing world, the practice spread in the 1980s and 1990s, when the personal computer became popular and exposed hacker culture to the world. CamelCase then became popular for business names. By 1990, it was very common to see CamelCase used in this way: (1962) PolyGram, formerly one of the major labels of the music industry. (1977) CompuServe, UnitedHealthCare (now UnitedHealthcare). (1979) MasterCard, SportsCenter, VisiCalc (1984) BellSouth, LaserJet, MacWorks, iDEN (1987) ClarisWorks, HyperCard, PowerPoint (1990) HarperCollins, SeaTac, iconic WorldWideWeb During the late 1990s when the internet became far more popular and easily available, the lowercase prefixes "e" (for "electronic") and "i" (for "Internet", "information", "interactive", "intelligent", etc.) became quite common, and we began to see names like Apple's iMac and the eBox computer program. The original name of the practice, used in media studies, grammars and the Oxford English Dictionary, was "medial capitals". The fancier names such as "InterCaps", "CamelCase" and other variations are recent and seem more common in computer-related communities. The earliest known occurrence of the term "InterCaps" on Usenet is in an April 1990 post to the group by Avi Rappoport, with "BiCapitalization" appearing slightly later in a 1991 post by Eric S. Raymond to the same group. The earliest use of the name "CamelCase" occurs in 1995, in a post by Newton Love. "With the advent of programming languages having these sorts of constructs, the humpiness of the style made me call it HumpyCase at first, before I settled on CamelCase. I had been calling it CamelCase for years," said Love, "The citation above was just the first time I had used the name on USENET." The use of medial caps for identifiers is recommended by many organizations and software projects. For some languages (such as Mesa, Pascal, Modula, Java and Microsoft's.NET) CamelCase is recommended by the language developers or by important manuals and has therefore become part of the language's "culture". Style guidelines often distinguish between upper and lower CamelCase. They usually specify which one should be used for certain kinds of things: variables, record fields, methods, procedures, types, etc. This is sometimes supported by static analysis tools that check source code to make sure it is following these guidelines. CamelCase is used in some wiki markup languages for terms that should be automatically linked to other wiki pages. This convention was originally used in Ward Cunningham's original wiki software, WikiWikiWeb, and can be activated in most other wikis. Some wiki engines such as TiddlyWiki, Trac and PMWiki use it in the default settings. They also usually provide an option or plugin to disable it. Wikipedia used to use CamelCase linking. However, they have switched to explicit link markup using square brackets and many other wiki sites have done the same. Some wikis that do not use CamelCase linking may still use the CamelCase as a naming convention, such as AboutUs. The NIEM registry requires that XML data elements use upper CamelCase and XML attributes use lower CamelCase. Most popular command-line interfaces and scripting languages usually can't handle file names that contain embedded spaces. Because of this, users of those systems often use CamelCase (or underscores, hyphens and other "safe" characters) for compound file names like. Microblogging and social networking sites that limit the number of characters in a message (most famously Twitter, where the 140-character limit can be quite restrictive in languages that rely on alphabets, including English) are usually outlets for medial capitals. Using CamelCase between words reduces the number of spaces, and thus the number of characters in a given message. This allows more content to fit into the limited space. CamelCase has been used in languages other than English for several purposes. Some examples are: CamelCase is sometimes used in the writing or translation of certain scripts as a way to tell the difference between certain letters or markings. An example is the rendering of Tibetan proper names like rLobsang: the "r" here stands for a prefix glyph in the original script that functions as tone marker rather than a normal letter. Another example is tsIurku, a Latin transcription of the Chechen term for the capping stone of the characteristic Medieval defensive towers of Chechenia and Ingushetia; the capital letter "I" here showing a phoneme different from the one transcribed as "i". CamelCase may also be used when writing proper names in languages that add prefixes to words. In some of those languages, the custom is to leave the prefix in lower case and capitalize the root. This convention is used in Irish orthography e.g., i nGaillimh ("in Galway"), from Gaillimh ("Galway"); go hÉireann ("to Ireland"), from Éire ("Ireland). Similarly, when translating the Hebrew language, haIvri means "the Hebrew person" and biYerushalayim means "in Jerusalem". This convention is also used by several Bantu languages (e.g., kiSwahili = "Swahili language", isiZulu = "Zulu language") and several indigenous languages of Mexico (e.g. Nahuatl, Totonacan, Mixe–Zoque and some Oto-Manguean languages). Abbreviations of some academic qualifications are sometimes presented in CamelCase without punctuation, e.g. PhD or BSc. In French, CamelCase acronyms such as OuLiPo (1960) were favored for a time as alternatives to initialisms (or representing compound words only by the first letter of each word). CamelCase is often used to transliterate initialisms into alphabets where two letters may be required to represent a single character of the original alphabet, e.g., DShK from Cyrillic ДШК and PPSh from Cyrillic ППШ. In Chinese pinyin, CamelCase is sometimes used for place names so that it is easier for readers to pick out the different parts of the word. For example, places like Beijing (北京) and Qinhuangdao (秦皇岛) and Daxing'anling (大兴安岭) can be written as BeiJing, QinHuangDao, and DaXingAnLing, with the number of capital letters being the same as the number of Chinese characters for each word. Writing word compounds only by the initial letter of each character is also acceptable in some cases, so Beijing can be written as BJ, Qinghuangdao as QHD, and Daxing'anling as DXAL. In several languages, including English, pronouns and possessives may be capitalized to show respect. For example: when referring to the reader of a formal letter or to God. In some of those languages, the capitalization is retained even when those words occur within compound words or suffixed to a verb. For example, in Italian one would write porgendoLe distinti saluti ("offering to You respectful salutations") or adorarLo ("adore Him"). In German nouns carry a grammatical gender—which, for roles or job titles, is usually masculine. Since the feminist movement of the 1980s, some writers and publishers have been using the feminine title suffixes -in (singular) and -innen (plural) to help boost the inclusion of women; but written with a capital 'I', to indicate that males are not excluded. Example: MitarbeiterInnen ("co-workers, female") instead of Mitarbeiter ("co-workers", masculine grammatical gender) or Mitarbeiterinnen ("female co-workers"). This use is analogous to the use of parentheses in English, for example in the phrase "congress(wo)man." In German, the names of statutes are shortened using embedded capitals. An example would be: StGB (Strafgesetzbuch) for criminal code, PatG (Patentgesetz) for Patent Act or the very common GmbH (Gesellschaft mit beschränkter Haftung) for Company with Limited Liability.

The family Campanulaceae (also bellflower family), of the order Asterales, contains about 70 genera and 2000 species, you are probably familiar with bellflowers and cardinal flower and think of these as a group of small herbaceous flowers.

Campbell's dwarf hamster (Phodopus campbelli) is a species of hamster. It is native to central Asia. The species was named after a man called W. C. Campbell, who collected the first one in Mongolia on 1 July 1902. They typically eat corn, oats, peanuts, vegetables and a wide variety of seeds. They also eat insects, arthropods mollusks, leaves, wood, bark, seeds, stems, flowers, fruits, and grains. The Campbell's dwarf hamster has predators like foxes, owls, eagles, kestrels, and falcons. Campbell's dwarf hamsters live about 2.5 years to 3 years. They live in burrows and use grass, feathers, and wool, to create it. Seeds and food are extremely close inside because they don’t want other animals to find their food source so that they can have enough food when it is time for winter. The Campbell's Russian hamster is a grayish color with a cream white belly and a dark stripe running down its back. There are 3 types of colors that have been identified. The collared, mottled, and the spot. They each vary and can be very different from another.

A trailer or vehicle accessory used for camping, see recreational vehicle, travel trailer or camper shell. A Campervan - a self-powered van converted for camping. a person who engages in camping. a reference to the alternative rock band named Camper Van Beethoven. in online games, a player who stays in one area of the game world, see camping (computer gaming). Camper, a shoe company from Majorca, Spain. a camper can be a term for one who stays in their vehicle for a long period of time. Petrus Camper, a Dutch anatomist.

Camphor is a waxy, flammable, transparent solid. It has a strong smell. It is a terpenoid. Its chemical formula is C10H16O. It is found in the wood of the camphor laurel (Cinnamomum camphora). Camphor can also be artificially made from the oil of turpentine.

The Canada lynx is a species of lynx which lives on the taiga. It is about twice the size of a domestic cat. It eats mice, ground squirrels, lemming and young deer. The lynx's favorite food is the snowshoe hare, which makes up 60% to 97% of its diet. This wild animal is not endangered (except in the southern 48 states of the US). It is of "least concern" (IUCN). Humans hunt them for their beautiful, thick fur. It has tufts on its ears whose function is probably social signalling.

Candida parapsilosis is a fungal species of yeast that has become a cause of sepsis and of wound and tissue infections in people who have immune system defects. Unlike Candida albicans and Candida tropicalis, C. parapsilosis is not an obligate human pathogen. C. parapsilosis normally lives on humans as a commensal yeast. It is one of the fungi most frequently isolated from human hands. There are several risk factors that can contribute to C. parapsilosis infection. Those with immune system diseases have a high risk of having a C. parapsilosis infection. These include surgical patients. There is currently no agreement on the treatment of invasive candidiasis caused by C. parapsilosis. The approach includes the removal of foreign bodies such as implanted prostheses. Medication is given to treat the infection. The use of antifungal therapy includes amphotericin B and fluconazole. Candida parapsilosis was discovered in Puerto Rico in 1928. Ashford collected it from a diarrheal stool. It was first named Monilia parapsilosis and was considered to not be the cause of infection. It was found to be a causative agent of sepsis in an intravenous drug user in 1940. It is now considered an important hospital disease caused by fungi. C. parapsilosis is the most common non-C. albicans species of Candida. It is the second most common pathogen in superficial candidiasis after C. albicans. C. parapsilosis is white, creamy, and shiny when grown on dextrose agar. Its cell shape is oval, round, or like a cylinder. When C. parapsilosis is found more often in nature than other species Candida. This is likely because it is one of the few species of the genus not restricted to humans. Invasive infection occurs often in low-birth weight newborn babies in the United States. And it is a bloodstream infection found in North America. It is most commonly found on human skin and is most frequently encountered in Asia and Latin America. It can make chemicals that will destroy the cells of other organisms. Endocarditis can be caused by C. parapsilosis in patients using having intravenous parenteral nutrition (6.9%) treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics (5.6%) The mortality rate is 41.7% to 61%. Ocular infection caused by C. parapsilosis has been found after cataract removal and with corticosteroid eye drop use. C. parapsilosis infection of the skin and gastrointestinal tract can occur.in which the production of pseudohyphae is associated with the elicitation of an inflammatory response. Candida parapsilosis is occasionally encountered in toenail fungus. Serious C. parapilosis infection is mostly due to the use of in-dwelling devices. It can stick to other organisms' cells. It can also adhere to tissue, especially mucosal surfaces. C. parapsilosis can be found with thin, unstructured biofilms. The existence of the fungus in a biofilm helps it resist antifungal treatment. Thus, adhesion to abiotic and biotic surfaces is often a precursor to serious infection. The risk of C. parapsilosis infection is increased in the setting of implanted medical devices, prostheses, and therapy with feeding solutions. Also, low-birth weight infants are at higher risk of sepsis from this species.

Canis is a genus with seven to ten living species. It incudes the domestic dog, wolves, coyotes, and jackals, and various extinct species. 'Canis' means "dog" in Latin. Their canine teeth are adapted for killing, and their molar teeth can crunch bone. They are able to chase prey over long distances, far more so than felines.

Cannabidiol (CBD) is one of the 150+ naturally occurring phytocannabinoids found in certain strains of hemp and in all cannabis plant strains. CBD is the abbreviated version of cannabidiol, which is one of the leading compound found in hemp plant, as naturally hemp has more CBD than any other compound found in its chemical composition. CBD is a cannabinoid, and due to their relationship with the body’s endocannabinoid system, it is a unique compounds from others, it uses cannabinoids to perform regulatory actions which affect our overall wellbeing. It is legal in many places and is used in the management and treatment of chronic pain, PTSD, anxiety, anxiety disorder, depression, diabetes type 1, diabetes type 2, seizures, and in conjunction with allopathic approaches to diseases including cancer chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Anecdotally CBD is being used with claimed positive results by patients for almost every illness. CBD, unlike Δ9-THC (Tetrahydrocannabinol), is a non psycho-active compound of cannabis. Its use and popularity as an alternative to pharmaceutical drugs is growing worldwide despite difficulties, ambiguities and, in some cases, contradictory legal status in some states and countries. In the USA the consumption of CBD hemp oil is federally legal, since CBD hemp oil falls under the same importation and commerce laws as other hemp products. Some US states have not enacted legislation specifically relating to CBD hemp oil and continue to use high THC cannabis laws to govern the status of CBD. At the same time many states have legislated to legalize or decriminalize cannabis. Most states have detailed information relating to the legal status of recreational cannabis, CBD, and what is increasingly referred to as 'medicinal cannabis'. up-to-date state specific info can be seen at Legal history of cannabis in the United States (in Notes). In 1939 Irishman William Brooke O'Shaughnessy introduced cannabis extract to American pharmacies and thus began it's popularity as a remedy. A wide range of cannabis extracts became freely available and could be gotten from travelling doctors, 'snake oil salesmen', and apothecaries across America and Europe. The general lack of controls and regulation at the time lead to some deaths and injuries linked back to supposed cannabis extracts. Unscrupulous makers produced formulations that were of questionable quality for quick profits and some cases the ingredients were toxic or poisonous. This unfortunate practice was widespread across the profitable field of medicine and remedies. As result, in 1906, The Pure Food and Drug Act was passed by the United States Congress. It required that certain special drugs, including cannabis extracts, be properly and correctly labeled with contents. Prior to this many drugs were marketed as 'patented' medicines with 'secret ingredients'. The new regulations, however, did nothing to stem criticism about the availability of narcotics in particular and around 1910 there was a new round of legislation aimed to strengthen requirements for their sale and remove 'loopholes' in poison laws. The 1910 revisions were designed to restrict all narcotics, including cannabis, as poisons therefore requiring a doctors prescription and limiting sales to pharmacies only. The first instance of the 1906 Act was enacted by the District of Columbia in the same year as 'An act to regulate the practice of pharmacy and the sale of poisons in the District of Columbia, and for other purposes'. The act was again updated in 1938 to the Federal Pure Food, Drug, and Cosmetics Act of 1938 which is still current as of the early 21st century. To date, marijuana remains under this law defined as a "dangerous drug". CBD as a separate substance or as an ingredient of other products is legal across the USA since it is a hemp extract however when purchasing people should check their specific local and national laws. Evidence suggests that hemp and cannabis may have been farmed for up to 12,000 years and had many uses including the making of cloth, rope, paper, food, and medicine. However, in the modern context, it was not until its introduction to American pharmacies by William Brooke O'Shaughnessy in 1839 that Cannabis extracts came into mainstream awareness as a medicine. A wide range of cannabis extracts became easily available and could be gotten from travelling doctors and salesmen, doctors, and drugstores throughout America. This ended the introduction of the Pure Food and Drug Act. Similar products were also available across Europe. In the early decades of the 21st century, CBD is again becoming well known for its qualities as a remedy for health problems. Its world-wide popularity is ahead of the slow process of making it legal to produce, supply, buy, and use cannabis for enjoyment in non-medical settings, and especially when it comes to CBD, which doesn't have a psycho-active component. There is some experience that CBD has a positive effect in managing and treating chronic pain, PTSD, anxiety, anxiety disorder, depression, diabetes type 1, diabetes type 2, seizures, and also combined with allopathic approaches to diseases including chemotherapy and radiation therapy for treating cancer. No toxic dose for CBD is known, and there is no record from any source of a death or serious injury from CBD as of this writing. CBD may be useful either as treatment for a specific illness or in a smaller dose for maintenance of good health. Usually, CBD is taken by mouth as oil drops or a powder that dissolves in water, or made into a food to be eaten. Another form of CBD is used on the skin as the oil or a cream to rub in. CBD is popularly taken in the 'vape' method (from the word "vapor"), with the CBD is heated so it can be inhaled. This method is favoured because the effect is felt sooner than by other means. Patients who need long-lasting relief from pain or other symptoms such as nausea, may combine two methods: for example, first vape and then eat a food made with CBD.

A cannabinoid is a chemical found in the cannabis (marijuana) plant. There are 113 cannabinoids that scientists know of, but there are likely more. Two of the best known cannabinoids are tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD). THC is a psychoactive drug, meaning it can make you feel and think differently. Not all cannabinoids are psychoactive and each one works differently. All cannabinoids share a similar chemical structure and are researched for treating diseases. Cannabinoids work by connecting, or binding, to receptors in the body. These receptors make up a system called the endocannabinoid system (ECS). There are two types of receptors: CB1 (cannabinoid receptor type 1) and CB2 (cannabinoid receptor type 2). CB1 receptors are mostly found in the central nervous system, which is made up of the brain and spine. It is also found in other places in the body like sex organs. CB2 is found in the peripheral nervous system in other parts of the body. CB2 receptors are found in the immune system, which is the system that prevents us from getting sick. Phytocannabinoids are cannabinoids that are found naturally in the cannabis plant are affected by light. They are different than synthetic cannabinoids that are made in a laboratory (lab).
